title: Winter and Bell
premise: Zephyrine Thackeray, a hospice nurse in the fen village of Marrowmere, has always heard the dying count backwards from an unknown number — and when the count reaches zero, they die. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins ringing again at night, Zephyrine discovers his own name appearing in a century-old hospice ledger written in his handwriting. The bell is a summons: the drowned congregation of 1911 is refilling the village well, one soul per toll, and the backwards counting is them being called home. To save the family he has found among the living — the widow Ada, her mute grandson Bell, and the other hospice patients — Zephyrine must falsify the ledger, striking their names out before the well refills, knowing the book will demand a substitute: himself. In the end he writes his own name last, lets the final toll take him, and wakes as the new keeper of the bell — remembered by no one except Bell, who finally speaks to say his name.
about_author: Astrid Kavanagh is a former palliative care chaplain who spent eleven years sitting with the dying in coastal Norfolk before turning to fiction. She writes horror about tenderness, insisting that grief is simply love with nowhere left to go.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Leaving
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. We meet him documenting the dying habits of his hospice patients, including the backwards counting no one else hears. He introduces Ada and her grandson Bell, who moved into the cottage next door after Ada's husband died under Zephyrine's care. Emotional beat: quiet loneliness soothed by ritual and the fragile warmth of found family.

chapters.title: A Bell That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. At 3 a.m. the church bell rings — but the tower is empty; the bell was melted for scrap in 1911. The villagers hear nothing. Only Zephyrine, and Bell, who points at the sky. That night, his first patient counts down faster than before. Emotional beat: dread entering a domestic space, the first crack in rational explanation.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Drowned Year
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Searching the parish archive, he finds a 1911 hospice ledger with entries in his own handwriting, dated decades before his birth, listing villagers who 'went to the water willingly.' The final page lists names still living — Ada's, Bell's, his own. Emotional beat: vertigo of identity dissolving; documentation becomes haunting rather than prayer.

chapters.title: What Bell Won't Say
chapters.summary: Bell's POV, rendered in close third with sparse interiority. Bell has not spoken since his grandfather's death, but he remembers the old man counting backwards and stopping mid-number. Bell draws the bell tower over and over, adding figures standing in the doorway. Emotional beat: the child as silent witness; found family deepening through shared fear.

chapters.title: Nine for the Well
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. A patient dies exactly as her count hits zero, and the well level rises measurably overnight. The vicar, Mr. Ellery, admits the parish has kept a 'tally' since 1911 and begs Zephyrine not to interfere. Nine names remain on the ledger. Emotional beat: complicity revealed; the horror is administrative, communal, patient.

chapters.title: The Counting Sickness
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Zephyrine and Ada. The remaining patients all begin counting in unison across separate rooms, synchronized like a tide. Ada confesses she came to Marrowmere fleeing something similar years ago and recognizes the pattern. Emotional beat: terror spreading through the household; Ada and Zephyrine bond as co-conspirators against fate.

chapters.title: Striking Out the Names
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. He attempts to cross the living names out of the 1911 ledger; the ink refuses, bleeding back. Each failed attempt makes the bell ring twice. He realizes the book accepts only substitutions — a name given freely. Emotional beat: desperation and moral clarity; he begins hiding the plan from Ada to spare her.

chapters.title: Zero Hour at Marrowmere
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The well brims; the bell rings without pause; the counting reaches single digits. Ada discovers Zephyrine's forged substitution pages and understands what he intends. She races to the church through floodwater rising in the lanes, Bell clinging to her back. Emotional beat: frantic love outrunning inevitability.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, climax. In the belfry, the drowned congregation of 1911 waits inside the sound itself. Zephyrine writes his own name into the ledger as the substitute and strikes the nine living names clean through. The final toll takes him mid-count — but he stops counting at one, refusing to reach zero, and the bell cracks. Emotional beat: sacrifice as authorship; he chooses the ending of his own record.

chapters.title: After the Refill
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, resolution. Spring comes; the well stays low; the cracked bell hangs silent. No one in Marrowmere remembers Zephyrine Thackeray except Bell, who stands at the empty belfry each evening and speaks his first word in two years: the nurse's name. Ada keeps the ledger, blank now, and begins writing new names in it — only the living. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into memory; found family enduring the cost of its making.
